:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(3)=2(3)=6,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt[4]{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt[4]{x}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{1}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-2.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-2\cdot (x-1) \\ y & =-2x+2+2 \\ y & =-2x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,2,0\,).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the $y$-intercept of the line that passes through the point $(-1, 4)$ and has a slope of $2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Since the line passes through the point $(-1,4)$ and its slope is $2$, we substitute $x=-1$, $y=4,$ and $m=2$ into the equation in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y &= mx + b \\
	(4) &= (2)(-1) + b \\
	4 &= -2 + b \\
	6 &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $y$-intercept is $b=6.$ The coordinates of the $y$-intercept are $(0,6).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the equation of the line that passes through the points $(-2,4)$ and $(10,10).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{10-4}{10-(-2)}=\frac{6}{12}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=\dfrac 1 2$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y = \dfrac 1 2 x + b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(10,10)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}x+b \\ 10 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10+b \\ 10 & =5+b \\ b & =10-5 \\ b & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is $y=\dfrac 1 2 x + 5.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the $x$-intercept of the line that passes through the point $(-3,2)$ and has a slope of $-\dfrac{1}{2}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the line. We know that $m=-\dfrac{1}{2},$ so we can write the equation of the line as $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x + b.$

It remains to find the $y$-intercept of the line. We can do that by substituting the point $(-3,2)$ into the equation and solving for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+b \\ (2) & =-\frac{1}{2}(-3)+b \\ 2 & =\frac{3}{2}+b \\ \frac{1}{2} & =b\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the line is $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+\dfrac{1}{2}.$

At the $x$-intercept, the $y$-coordinate is equal to $0.$ So, we can substitute $y=0$ into the equation and then solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & =-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $x=1.$ The coordinates of the $x$-intercept are $(1,0).$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the X-Intercept of a Line Given a Point and a Slope

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: A vertical line $l$ passes through the point $(-6,3).$ Calculate the coordinates of the $x$-intercept of $l.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
On any vertical line, all points have the same $x$-coordinate.

The $x$-coordinate of the point $(-6,3)$ is $-6,$ so the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept is also $-6.$

Therefore, the coordinates of the $x$-intercept are $(-6,0).$
